assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data research on intergenerational mobility has transformed measurement of equality of opportunity and made place, institutions, and childhood environments central empirical questions.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren, and Friedman are central to the linked-data mobility agenda; the broad collaborative nature of the work makes the three-person limit a real constraint.
assessment.maturity: The research program is well established, extensively used, and has already reshaped public-economics research and policy discussion.
uncertainties: The full contribution extends beyond the proposed three laureates, including Lawrence F. Katz and many collaborators.
Long-run interpretation of observed mobility patterns remains an active research area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work supplied a compelling empirical account of how technology, trade exposure, task change, and local adjustment shape labour demand and inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson form a clear core for the trade-shock and task-based evidence; Katz is also an important contributor to the broader literature.
assessment.maturity: Its methods and findings have had durable influence across labour, trade, regional, and political-economy research.
uncertainties: Separating the independent effects of trade, technology, and other local shocks is inherently difficult.
The candidate grouping combines related but distinguishable research programs.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The reconstruction of long-run income and wealth distributions, including offshore wealth, has changed the empirical basis for studying inequality and fiscal capacity.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are foundational in the modern top-income program, with Zucman a major contributor on wealth and international concealment.
assessment.maturity: The agenda has generated enduring data infrastructure and a large international research literature, with clear relevance to historical and contemporary inequality.
uncertainties: Capitalization, wealth valuation, and offshore-asset measurement require consequential assumptions.
The appropriate credit allocation spans a wider international data-network.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on agglomeration, cities, housing, and spatial allocation has provided a powerful account of why economic activity clusters and how places affect opportunity and growth.
assessment.attribution: Glaeser, Moretti, and Puga have especially central and complementary roles, though Duranton and Gyourko also represent major parts of the proposed contribution.
assessment.maturity: The core mechanisms and empirical tools are mature and influential in urban, regional, labour, and growth research.
uncertainties: The broad field includes several partially separable contributions.
Causal identification of place effects and housing constraints remains contested in particular applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evolutionary analysis of routines and organizational capabilities supplied a lasting alternative framework for understanding innovation, firm behavior, and economic dynamism.
assessment.attribution: Winter is a central figure in the specified contribution, although the intellectual tradition is closely associated with work beyond the single credited name.
assessment.maturity: The contribution has had decades to diffuse across organizational economics, innovation studies, and strategy.
uncertainties: The long intellectual lineage makes boundaries of the prizeable discovery difficult to draw.
Its influence is substantial but more dispersed across disciplines than some empirical programs.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The measurement and analysis of management practices made organizational quality and intangible productive capacity empirically tractable determinants of firm and national productivity.
assessment.attribution: Bloom and Van Reenen are the principal founders of the empirical management agenda, with Sadun an important contributor to its extension and institutional analysis.
assessment.maturity: The research has accumulated broad cross-country evidence and stimulated work linking management, technology, and productivity.
uncertainties: Management measures may partly capture other firm characteristics.
Experimental and observational evidence varies across settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework sharpened understanding of how distorted allocation across firms can explain large productivity and income differences.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are especially central to the quantitative empirical framework, while Restuccia is a key contributor to the broader misallocation literature.
assessment.maturity: The approach is widely used in development and growth accounting and has motivated substantial follow-up work.
uncertainties: Inference about underlying distortions from observed wedges is model-dependent.
The empirical magnitude and interpretation of misallocation remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm-heterogeneity trade models recast trade theory around selection, productivity, and within-industry reallocation, yielding a more empirically useful account of trade gains.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the pivotal originator of the core model, while Helpman and Redding made major contributions to its development and application.
assessment.maturity: The framework has become standard in international-trade research and supports a large empirical literature.
uncertainties: Credit for adjacent heterogeneous-firm and quantitative-trade contributions is necessarily broader than three people.
Quantifying welfare gains depends on strong modeling and measurement choices.
